stimulus: Brenwick's water mains began bursting in the winter of 1871; the inquiry that followed is our subject. Its tests told a simple story: every failed pipe came from a single casting run — the foundry's autumn pour, brittle across all samples — while pipe from other runs in the same streets never failed. The trenches sat in natural gravel that had never been disturbed; the new engines were metered, and pressure never rose past the old maximum; and the bursts came in August as often as in January — so much for frost. Notice, though, the inquiry's stamina: chartered for six months, it sat for five years, long after the public anger had died away — that persistence is the real lesson. Its yard tests were matched deliberately to buried conditions; not one gauge of its own went into the ground — the panel worked from testimony; and the laborers were examined as suspects. Why the rival company across the river? Rates. A decade of undercutting had poisoned everything, and the city would not fund repairs whose cost would surface in that rate war — that is why the money stalled. No one from the rival sat on the panel, the rival never bid for the works — the city itself absorbed them in the end — and the report went to the printers on schedule. The recommendations? Hamburg and Turin wrote them into practice within five years; at home they were never written into any code of the period, not even for the new districts, and when steel mains arrived the testing rules carried over unchanged.

options.D: The failures traced back to a single flawed casting run at the foundry

stimulus: Madariaga spent three years inside the Solana wholesale market, and the study still shapes how we think about informal order. His conclusion on the prized corner positions: seniority. Years on the floor decided who moved up when a pitch fell vacant — an order everyone could recite and nobody had written down. Not kinship: sons ranked behind longer-tenured newcomers, and the best pitches did not run in families. Not chance: he hunted for a lottery and found the traders laughing at the idea. Not hidden favors either: the fee books enter every transfer, dated, each matching the seniority queue exactly. Now, the months behind a stall of his own. Readers long puzzled over the silence in his field notes; the explanation is homely — minding the stall left no hand free to write, and the gap is exactly those months. The committee never admitted him; the account before and after keeps its cool distance perfectly; and the pre-dawn auctions he never saw — his stock came by consignment at midday. Bahn's objection, that the traveling vendors are missing, I concede: the census sheets stop at the permanent stalls. And Bahn's list was compiled in the study's final year. But the matters at issue were the fixed positions, where the travelers held no claim, and the omission leaves the central claim standing. The move to the new hall in 1954 is the coda: within a year the surrounding streets held more stalls than the hall did, the city's numbered plan inside was ignored from the first week, the seniority order never re-formed indoors, and not one dispute reached the municipal courts.

stimulus: Vaissalu's drawings, set beside the stones that still stand. He drew some forty memorials in the seventeen nineties; nine of those stones survive. The comparison isn't flattering. The letterforms he gives are wrong in the same places an earlier antiquarian, Rennik, had gone wrong — same bind-runes, same swallowed vowel. He was copying Rennik's sketchbook, not the stone. Two things he's innocent of, mind: where a stone had flaked, he leaves a gap, honestly blank; and his churchyard attributions hold up wherever we can test them. How did I come to this? The parsonage at Kolgama. I catalogued its library as a student, one wet summer, and there was Rennik's sketchbook. That's the whole connection — no squeezes have ever come out of that house, the glebe wall there is nineteenth-century brick, and Kolgama's own pastors kept none of the visitation books that first mention the stones. The dating quarrel now. Hallik dates the group later than the years carved on it. I'd narrow that. One carver, the Ansu master, worked late, and his pieces colour how the rest get read; I would not extend that to the group. The formulas are common regional ones, older than any printed model I know, and the stone there weathers fast, so I don't rest a case on weathering. Twenty-odd stones are unlocated. We won't print a text nobody has seen on the stone, and they stay in the corpus volume, marked missing. A handlist goes to the county museums; some may sit unrecognized in a storeroom. The radio appeal was tried upriver and turned up little but field boulders.

options.D: Where the surface had flaked, he supplied plausible letters of his own without marking them as guesses

stimulus: The nineteen-oh-seven earthquake, then, and what re-reading the old sheets does to it. Start with the logbook from the Luhemaa station. It is a weather book as much as an instrument book, and that is why it earned its keep. A low background rumble sits on the Luhemaa traces that autumn, and the daily wind and sea entries let us set storm surf aside as its source — the rumble is loudest on flat, still days. The observer's felt account went to a newspaper the same week; the logbook closes in the same year the official history gives; and the crate surfaced through a museum's accession list, not through anything in the logbook. Tammik has argued for two ruptures minutes apart, and Oks thinks the magnitude drops once you model those old instruments. Neither holds: the trace shows one rupture, and the magnitude barely moves. The source sits under the coastal parish the catalogues name. What changes is the damage — the river towns stand on soft alluvium, and that, more than the size of the shock, drew the map of ruin. The sheets survive nearly complete. Hardly a sheet is missing from the years the network changed hands, the years before nineteen fifteen are as thickly covered as any, and each sheet carries its station's stamp. The trouble is framing: someone trimmed the margins off for display, and the time marks went with them. Kolmsaare? I am persuaded. The aftershocks sit along its mapped trend. The northern structure fits the uplift no better, these are not scattered shocks in healed crust, and the Kolmsaare structure is young.

stimulus: The Vantsi roll — nine metres of notation, and the question everyone asks first: which staging is this? My answer is the plain one. It is the first staging. Look at the ensemble figures: thirty-two dancers crammed into the downstage third, exactly the crowding the opening reviews complained of. The ensemble numbers here are not thinned, they are packed. Nor is this a drill book — the roll follows one evening's order straight through — and the entrances are in the same ink and the same hand as the figures, so nobody redrew them for a later season. What does it actually record? The corps, in detail. Their steps are written out in full, each number carried through to its end. The soloists get a line of description apiece, no more. And the mime scenes are passed over in a phrase, where later notations linger on them. Now the wrapper. There is a customs stamp on it, and three articles have built an itinerary out of that stamp. The stamp dates a crate of linen thread, not the roll's journey; the wrapper is freight paper somebody reused, and the address on it has sent people to the wrong city. Wrapper and roll are of a piece, the same decade, and the stamp is a western port's. Next? We are going to dance it. One suite, with students, in the spring — the performance is the test. The order of the numbers is not in doubt, so the orchestral parts can wait, the rubbed passages were already read under raking light last winter, and the ballroom manuals are somebody else's project.

options.A: She endorses it for the figures, though she takes the entrances to have been redrawn for a later season
options.B: She endorses the claim, finding in the ensemble figures the crowded groupings the first reviews complained of
options.C: She reads it as a teaching document, setting down what dancers were drilled on rather than any staging given
options.D: She reads the roll as a record of the revival, with the ensemble numbers already thinned

stimulus: The Vantsi roll — nine metres of notation, and the question everyone asks first: which staging is this? My answer is the plain one. It is the first staging. Look at the ensemble figures: thirty-two dancers crammed into the downstage third, exactly the crowding the opening reviews complained of. The ensemble numbers here are not thinned, they are packed. Nor is this a drill book — the roll follows one evening's order straight through — and the entrances are in the same ink and the same hand as the figures, so nobody redrew them for a later season. What does it actually record? The corps, in detail. Their steps are written out in full, each number carried through to its end. The soloists get a line of description apiece, no more. And the mime scenes are passed over in a phrase, where later notations linger on them. Now the wrapper. There is a customs stamp on it, and three articles have built an itinerary out of that stamp. The stamp dates a crate of linen thread, not the roll's journey; the wrapper is freight paper somebody reused, and the address on it has sent people to the wrong city. Wrapper and roll are of a piece, the same decade, and the stamp is a western port's. Next? We are going to dance it. One suite, with students, in the spring — the performance is the test. The order of the numbers is not in doubt, so the orchestral parts can wait, the rubbed passages were already read under raking light last winter, and the ballroom manuals are somebody else's project.
question: [Academic Talk — Dance History] Why does the professor mention the customs stamp on the roll's wrapper?

options.A: It shows the wrapper is reused freight paper, so the address on it has misled earlier researchers
options.B: It fixes a border crossing that puts the roll in the company's baggage on its final tour
options.C: It dates the wrapper decades after the roll, showing the two traveled separately before being joined
options.D: It shows the roll entered the country from the south, not with the company returning from the west

stimulus: Sarvela's beetles — eleven thousand pins, and questions the specimens cannot settle. Start with the coastal meadows. The literature says Kepsara's ground beetle vanished around nineteen ten. Rehepapp takes that at face value. Ilves says the older records are misidentified relatives, since the sister species was not split off until the fifties and much of the coastal literature predates the split — a fair worry. But I have been through the trays: the old specimens are there, and they are correctly named. Nor did the beetle shift inland: the drained margins have been swept, and swept well, since the sixties. The post-war sweeping in the meadows themselves amounts to two afternoons. What thins out around nineteen ten is the collecting, not the beetle. The nineteen-oh-four auction catalogue. One copy carries a pencil note naming the buyer, whose heirs gave us the material — that is how the chain closes. Its lot descriptions run to a line each, too thin to match a box against, the prices in it are steep for the day, and the cabinet it lists came to the museum with the rest. The labels. There is no pencil under the ink; one hand wrote the coastal labels and its abbreviations don't vary; the oldest hand is Sarvela's own, from his school years. What the writing shows is a nineteen-thirties re-curation: a good many labels rewritten, the old spellings quietly modernized. Next: not re-pinning, the pins stay where Sarvela put them; not sequencing, we won't cut them; not the traded duplicates, Vaher published that list years ago. The mites that ride on these beetles — nobody has looked.

options.A: He is persuaded, noting that later collectors worked the same meadows hard and came back without it
options.B: He thinks the older records rest on misidentified relatives, so there is no disappearance to explain
options.C: He suspects the species moved into the drained margins nearby, where nobody thought to sweep
options.D: He argues the apparent disappearance tracks where collectors went, not where the beetle lived

stimulus: Turvaste — three parish volumes, and the crisis years at their centre. What the registers show is not a parish dying evenly. The burials fall heavily on households that had arrived within the previous decade, cottagers, hired men, families off the road, while the long-settled farms came through comparatively lightly. Not departure: the town lists show no bulge of arrivals from here in those years. Not two waves either — the burials run in one long swell. And the hamlets and the church village lost at much the same rate. Now, the entries. Halliste built a good deal on the cause column, and Piir on the lists at the back, both worth having: each says the register shapes what we think we see. But the cause column runs right through the crisis, and stillbirths are entered in the main sequence. The entries give a name and a farm, and leave the messenger out. The close reading shows the clerk wrote up several days at a time, so the day-by-day dating everyone quotes is ours, not the parish's. The eighteen-eighties rebinding. The margins came through it uncut, no bill for the work has been found, and the covers went back on plain. What did happen is that a few leaves from the parish upriver were bound in by mistake, and nobody caught it until the nineteen thirties. Next? Not the rent rolls, Turvaste's burned in the eighteen forties. Not the neighbours, whose registers are in poor shape. Grain prices are already in the appendix of my first article. I want the slow method: reconstituting a sample of households in full.

options.A: The crisis came in two waves a year apart, and the second was the heavier one

options.C: The parish lost people mainly to departure, with households leaving for the towns rather than dying
options.D: Losses fell hardest on the outlying hamlets, while the church village itself was less touched

stimulus:
Kuivalinn hall came down in nineteen sixty-one. What survives is Rebasmaa's notebooks, eleven recordings, and Nommiste's drawings. Rebasmaa measured with pistol shots fired from the stage, logged position by position across two evenings. He had asked the mill to send workers in to fill the seats; the mill declined, so the hall stood empty for both sittings. What he entered are the single readings themselves, not averages; no cards stand behind them. The hall was renovated in fifty-four and he did not go back, so that book holds one campaign, not two.

Was the sound as fine as its reputation? I think so: a modern designer would still envy the measured values. The memoirists came late and added little. The resident orchestra was a middling band that toured to no acclaim. And these figures are not the long reverberation that period taste supposedly prized - they are short and defined.

Now the recordings. Cleaned digitally, they can anchor a computed model of the room, which no drawing on its own could support. The players were shifted between takes with no note kept, so the discs will not fix anybody's placement, and the room's contribution sits well above the surface noise once cleaned. The studio discs are a different decade and a different orchestra.

Next, then. Rebuilding a length of that wall at full scale was costed and is beyond us; the museum will mount its exhibition without our help; the local press we have read through already. Nommiste's smaller hall at Harmavere still stands, and we will measure it as our stand-in.

options.C: Readings were taken with the seats filled by workers from a nearby factory, given the afternoon off for it
options.D: Rebasmaa repeated the series after a renovation, and both campaigns are written up in the same book
